implementation_notes: Rust has no observer type and the borrow checker forbids a subject holding &mut Observer, so the realization is hand-written: the registry stores Arc'd closures (or trait objects) behind an Arc<RwLock<...>>, subscribe() inserts and returns an id, and notify() clones the handler Arcs under a short read lock, releases the lock and only then calls them. This ownership discipline is the price of the pattern in Rust: no garbage collector, no implicit weak listeners, no ambient mutability. Channels (std::sync::mpsc, tokio broadcast) are the alternative when subscribers are tasks rather than objects.
pitfalls: A closure that captures an Arc to the subject (or a strong reference to it) creates a reference cycle: the subject owns the handler and the handler owns the subject - capture Weak or break the cycle in unsubscribe.
Holding the RwLock guard across the callback deadlocks as soon as a handler subscribes or notifies; clone the handles and drop the guard first (as above).

Unsubscribe only removes the entry, so a handler can still run once from an in-flight notification snapshot: a subscription handle should be documented as best-effort, and re-entrant subscriptions must be idempotent.
Unbounded registries leak silently: forgetting to unsubscribe (or dropping a subscription handle without running its Drop, e.g. after mem::forget) keeps the closure and its captures alive.

variants.name: tokio::sync::broadcast (bounded multi-consumer channel)
variants.implementation_notes: In async Rust the structure is usually replaced by a channel: broadcast::channel(capacity) returns a Sender that can be cloned, every subscriber gets its own Receiver via Sender::subscribe(), each sent value is delivered to all active receivers in send order, and a receiver that falls behind is told through RecvError::Lagged instead of blocking the publisher. Notification becomes pull-from-a-stream (select! or StreamExt::next), which fits ownership, gives explicit backpressure semantics and removes the mutable registry entirely. Use the closure registry when notification must be synchronous; use broadcast when subscribers are tasks.
pitfalls: A slow receiver lags and misses messages (RecvError::Lagged) rather than applying backpressure; capacity is rounded up to a power of two and is the only buffer, so size it for the worst subscriber.
Subscribing after a send misses earlier values: a receiver is a stream, not a snapshot of current state.
Dropping every Sender closes the channel and ends all receivers with RecvError::Closed; send() returns Err(SendError) when no receiver exists, which is a normal condition, not a panic.
